quote: I know that one at a time is more. But I'd say, like, $2.50 average. Around $2.50 average, you said.
stewart_read: The bill figure was captured but the transcription '$2.50' is almost certainly a Deepgram mis-transcription of '$250' — a monthly bill of $2.50 is not plausible. Regardless of the exact figure, the rep captured a number and moved straight to the next verify item without acknowledging or flipping it into pain-based leverage.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep could have treated the ambiguous or garbled figure as low-value data and reasonably deprioritized it in favor of moving quickly through a customer who was in a hurry (per 01:32 'we won't be' home much longer) — but this doesn't explain why no acknowledgment of any kind followed.
coaching_implication: Manager should note that whatever number the customer says, the rep should audibly acknowledge it ('okay, so you're paying around $250 a month') before moving on — both to confirm accuracy against transcription errors and to bank it as leverage.

quote: Okay. And then do you have a credit score over 6 70?
stewart_read: Rep used the schema's stated 670 threshold correctly (unlike the drift observed in other calls where 650 was used), and moved on immediately once the customer confirmed.
coaching_implication: No coaching action needed here — this is a clean, correct qualifier ask matching schema.

quote: I have metal. One part of newer. One part, a 100 years old.
stewart_read: The customer disclosed part of the roof is '100 years old,' which under dq_rules could trigger a re-roof-required flag, yet the rep did not probe further (age of newer section, condition, or replacement plans) before moving to the credit qualifier.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged the 'newer' portion sufficient for a viable install area and reasonably let the closer sort out roof specifics — a legitimate scope-discipline call rather than a miss, since detailed roof engineering assessment is closer/specialist territory.
coaching_implication: Manager should have the rep at minimum note down 'roof has an old section' for the handoff so the closer isn't surprised, and consider one follow-up question on which section would host panels.

stewart_read: The customer confirmed a co-owner (wife) on the title. This is a factual answer to a qualification question, not a spousal-deferral objection, so no persuasion was needed — but the rep never followed up to include her on the appointment.
coaching_implication: Since the wife is a co-owner, she should be looped into the appointment per the spirit of protocols.spouse_decision even though this wasn't raised as an objection. Manager should coach the rep to proactively ask 'will she be able to join the call too?' whenever a co-owner is identified, not only when the customer raises it as a barrier.

quote: If I text you, could you just take a picture of that graph it has, and then we'll be good to get you talking to a specialist.
stewart_read: Rep explained the purpose of the bill (kWh usage history) clearly and gave the customer a concrete, low-friction action (photo via text), which is the correct move per the schema's bill_collection template.
coaching_implication: This is a positive example the manager can point to — clear, simple bill-collection framing that resolved the customer's 'why do you need it' pushback in one line.

quote: Let's see. If we call you at one, is that okay?
stewart_read: Rep offered a specific time and adjusted when the customer pushed back, landing on 3PM — this is a reasonable negotiation rather than a passive close.
coaching_implication: Good time-anchoring behavior; manager can note this as a strength but should also flag that the button-up lacked the fuller required elements (see coaching_focus).

quote: Alright. You too. Alright. You guys enjoy your day, and thank you for everything.
stewart_read: The call ends with a day and time locked (tomorrow 3PM) and a promised confirmation text, but the rep never ran the full button-up: no one-hour block statement, no 'not driving / at a computer' instruction, and no explicit 'is that fair?' handshake.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged the call already ran long with app/bill friction and wanted to end efficiently rather than risk over-talking a customer who twice pushed for a later time — a legitimate time-management call, but it still leaves the appointment more fragile than a full button-up would.
coaching_implication: Manager should drill the full button-up checklist (hour block, no-driving/computer instruction, 'is that fair?') as a closing habit regardless of how smoothly the rest of the call went — this is what protects the show rate.
